inference_time_prompt_injection.title: 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
inference_time_prompt_injection.text:
## 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking

The research landscape of Large Language Model (LLM) security, specifically concerning prompt injection and jailbreak attacks, underwent a rapid and transformative evolution between 2025 and 2026. This period is characterized by a definitive shift from static, rule-based, and single-model defensive paradigms toward a highly dynamic, automated, and co-evolutionary adversarial arms race [l2_Prompt Injection_v100]. In the early phases of 2025, the literature reflected a growing consensus that static defenses were fundamentally inadequate against sophisticated adversaries. Researchers demonstrated that existing guardrails could be consistently bypassed by employing adaptive optimization techniques. During this phase, the offensive state-of-the-art advanced significantly through the application of modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms, which achieved alarming Attack Success Rates (ASR) ranging from 50% to 71% against state-of-the-art LLM agents [Zhan_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_LLM, Maloyan_2025_LLM]. As 2025 progressed, this temporal trend bifurcated into two distinct but interconnected trajectories: the exploitation of complex agentic environments and the pursuit of extreme computational efficiency for attackers [l2_Prompt Injection_v100].

### 5.1 Exploitation of Agentic Environments

The integration of external tools into LLM agents introduced severe security risks, most notably Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), where adversaries embed malicious instructions into external data sources rather than direct user inputs [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Zhan et al. (2025) conducted the first comprehensive evaluation of existing IPI defenses against adaptive attacks in LLM agents. They adapted established jailbreak strategies specifically for the IPI setting, assuming white-box access to optimize adversarial strings that maximize the probability of the LLM generating a specific target response, such as a ReAct thought process or a JSON function call [Zhan_2025_LLM]. To bypass specific defenses, the authors introduced specialized variants: Multi-objective GCG (M-GCG) adds a stealth objective to evade detection-based defenses by jointly or iteratively optimizing to misclassify the attack as benign; Two-stage GCG (T-GCG) targets paraphrasing defenses by training a two-part string where the paraphraser's output matches the target trigger; and AutoDAN generates semantically meaningful adversarial strings to bypass Perplexity Filtering [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Their empirical results demonstrated that eight different state-of-the-art defenses could be consistently bypassed, achieving an ASR of over 50% and highlighting the critical necessity of incorporating adaptive attack evaluations when designing agent guardrails [Zhan_2025_LLM].

Building upon the need to uncover vulnerabilities in black-box agent architectures, Wang et al. (2025) proposed AGENTVIGIL, the first generic, automated black-box fuzzing framework designed to discover and exploit IPI vulnerabilities [Wang_2025_LLM]. AGENTVIGIL overcomes the challenges of sparse, binary feedback inherent in black-box systems by utilizing a high-quality initial seed corpus of adversarial prompt templates and an MCTS-based seed selection algorithm [Wang_2025_LLM]. Specifically, the framework employs the Upper Confidence Bound 1 (UCB1) algorithm to balance the exploration of new prompt variants and the exploitation of high-scoring seeds. A helper LLM then acts as a mutator, applying one of five basic mutation strategies—Shorten, Expand, Rephrase, Crossover, or GenerateSimilar—to the selected seed [Wang_2025_LLM]. To maximize the optimization signal, AGENTVIGIL employs an adaptive seed scoring strategy that calculates a final score based on a hybrid metric combining the ASR with other relevant factors [Wang_2025_LLM]. This automated attack methodology achieved remarkable success, recording ASRs of 70% to 71% against agents powered by o3-mini and GPT-4o on public benchmarks like AgentDojo and VWA-adv [Wang_2025_LLM]. Furthermore, the practical applicability of these attacks was validated in real-world environments, where the framework successfully misled web agents into navigating to arbitrary and malicious URLs [Wang_2025_LLM].

### 5.2 Automated Attacks via Genetic Algorithms

The automated generation of adversarial prompts also extended to LLM-as-a-judge systems, which are increasingly deployed to evaluate text quality, code correctness, and argument strength [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Maloyan et al. (2025) investigated the vulnerability of these evaluation systems, distinguishing between content-author attacks, where malicious text is submitted for evaluation, and system-prompt attacks, where the evaluation template itself is compromised [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Drawing insights from the "LLMs: You Can't Please Them All" Kaggle competition, they identified practical attack strategies such as Complex Word Bombardment, which induces cognitive overload [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. To systematize these vulnerabilities, they developed a framework building upon the HOUYI approach, consisting of a Framework Component, a Separator Component, and a Disruptor Component [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Within this framework, they introduced the Adaptive Search-Based Attack (ASA), a novel approach utilizing genetic algorithms to optimize attack strings based on model feedback [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Through rigorous evaluation across five models, including frontier models like GPT-4 and Claude-3-Opus, the authors demonstrated that sophisticated attacks could achieve success rates up to 73.8% [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Notably, smaller open-source models such as Gemma-3-4B-Instruct proved significantly more vulnerable, exhibiting a 65.9% average success rate, while multi-model committees with diverse architectures were shown to reduce attack success rates by 20 to 47 percentage points [Maloyan_2025_LLM].

### 5.3 The Pursuit of Extreme Computational Efficiency

Concurrently, the offensive landscape saw a paradigm shift toward extreme computational efficiency. A critical turning point was the introduction of knowledge distillation techniques to transfer jailbreaking capabilities from massive LLMs to highly efficient Small Language Models (SLMs) [Slms_2025_Efficient]. The Adversarial Prompt Distillation (APD) framework pioneered this asymmetric warfare tactic by integrating masked language modeling, KL divergence loss, and dynamic temperature control within a Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) optimization loop [Slms_2025_Efficient]. By distilling the adversarial capabilities of high-capacity teacher models, such as Llama-3.1-8B, into lightweight student models like BERT and RoBERTa, attackers could generate adversarial inputs 3.7 times faster than traditional LLM-based attacks [Slms_2025_Efficient]. This approach not only significantly reduced generation time and memory demands but also maintained an exceptionally high ASR of over 96%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art jailbreak methods in both harmfulness and stealthiness [Slms_2025_Efficient]. Consequently, the defensive community was forced to pivot away from computationally heavy semantic models toward more agile solutions [l2_Prompt Injection_v100].

### 5.4 Co-evolutionary and Dynamic Defenses

In response to these automated and highly efficient attacks, the defensive community developed dynamic, co-evolutionary systems. Liu et al. (2025) proposed AEGIS, an Automated co-Evolutionary framework for Guarding prompt Injections Schema [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Inspired by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), AEGIS systematically evolves both attackers and defenders in an iterative, two-level optimization process, providing adaptive robustness against prompt injection attacks [Liu_2025_Aegis]. In the outer loop, an Attacker module and a Defender module alternate turns, while the inner loop utilizes TGO+, an enhanced textual gradient optimization module tailored for black-box LLMs [Liu_2025_Aegis]. TGO+ leverages multi-route textual gradients—generating gradients based on multiple optimization metrics simultaneously—and gradient buffering to simulate gradient-like updates using natural language feedback without requiring model fine-tuning [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Evaluated on a real-world automated assignment grading application, AEGIS improved the True Positive Rate (TPR) of malicious prompt detection by 0.20 compared to previous state-of-the-art methods, confirming the critical role of co-evolution, gradient replay, and multi-objective optimization in modern defense strategies [Liu_2025_Aegis].

Alongside co-evolutionary frameworks, researchers developed lightweight, real-time moderation systems to mitigate the computational overhead of continuous defense. Zhang et al. (2025) introduced RTST (Real-Time Self-Tuning), a multi-agent moderator framework designed to defend against jailbreaks without requiring expensive retraining [Zhang_2025_Real]. RTST employs a parallel architecture where a Main Model and an Evaluator agent assess prompts against a tunable JSON 'Behavior Set' that assigns base scores to specific prompt criteria [Zhang_2025_Real]. Specialized Reviewer agents handle potential false positives and false negatives, allowing the system to self-tune in real-time by adjusting behavior weights or adding new adversarial criteria [Zhang_2025_Real]. Similarly, Li et al. (2025) proposed SecurityLingua, a plug-and-play defense framework utilizing security-oriented prompt compression [Li_2025_LLM]. By training a Transformer encoder on a high-quality 221K-example dataset to extract the true intention of adversarial prompts, SecurityLingua passes the compressed intention via the system prompt while keeping the original user prompt intact [Li_2025_LLM]. This two-step mechanism stimulates built-in safety guardrails, achieving a 1% average jailbreak success rate with negligible computational overhead, requiring approximately 32 extra tokens and 25ms of latency [Li_2025_LLM].

Exploring alternative defensive paradigms, Corll et al. (2026) introduced Mirror, a reusable data-curation design pattern that treats prompt injection defense as a geometric engineering task rather than a semantic modeling problem [Corll_2026_Mirror]. By organizing the training corpus into matched positive and negative cells across nuisance dimensions such as language, length, topic, and format, Mirror prevents classifiers from learning spurious shortcuts [Corll_2026_Mirror]. The system defines a 32-cell topology covering various attack reasons and languages. A sparse character word-boundary n-gram Linear SVM trained on 5,000 strictly curated samples substantially outperformed a 22M-parameter transformer baseline, Prompt Guard 2, operating with submillisecond latency and no external model runtime dependencies [Corll_2026_Mirror].

### 5.5 Prompt Interactions and the "Think Mode Paradox"

Finally, the interaction between prompt-based defenses and in-context learning emerged as a critical area of study for understanding residual vulnerabilities. Wang et al. (2026) conducted the first systematic investigation of interaction effects between few-shot demonstrations and system prompt strategies [Wang_2026_LLM]. They discovered a divergent interaction effect: few-shot demonstrations enhanced Role-Oriented Prompts (RoP) by up to 4.5%, but degraded Task-Oriented Prompts (ToP) by up to 21.2% [Wang_2026_LLM]. To explain these phenomena, the authors developed a mathematical framework based on Bayesian in-context learning to model 'role reinforcement' for RoP, and utilized attention analysis—incorporating softmax attention entropy and the 'lost in the middle' position bias—to model 'attention dilution' for ToP [Wang_2026_LLM]. Furthermore, the authors identified the "think mode paradox," revealing that reasoning-enhanced models exhibit higher vulnerability to both jailbreak attacks and negative few-shot interactions [Wang_2026_LLM]. These findings underscore the complexity of deploying prompt-based defenses and highlight the necessity of carefully pairing few-shot examples with appropriate system prompt architectures to ensure optimal safety [Wang_2026_LLM].

inference_time_threats_adversarial.text:
Here is the drafted section for your survey paper, focusing on inference-time adversarial attacks, domain-specific vulnerabilities, healthcare security, and advanced detection mechanisms.

***

# Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks

The deployment of deep neural networks (DNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications has exposed a critical vulnerability surface during the inference phase. Unlike training-time threats, such as data poisoning or backdoor injections, inference-time threats assume the model's parameters are fixed and attempt to manipulate the model's output by carefully crafting the input data. Among these threats, adversarial attacks remain one of the most prominent and extensively studied areas in AI security. This section explores the landscape of inference-time adversarial attacks, examining how they manifest in domain-specific contexts—particularly in the high-stakes realm of healthcare—and detailing advanced defensive paradigms such as stateful detection and contrastive prompt tuning.

## 1. The Landscape of Adversarial Attacks

Adversarial attacks are broadly categorized into white-box and black-box settings, depending on the adversary's knowledge of the target model. In a white-box scenario, the attacker has full access to the model's architecture, weights, and gradients, allowing for the precise calculation of adversarial perturbations using techniques like gradient ascent. However, in most commercial and deployed systems, models are hidden behind APIs, restricting attackers to a black-box setting. 

In these black-box environments, adversaries frequently rely on query-based attacks. Query-based black-box adversarial attacks estimate adversarial gradients based on the returned probability vectors (or logits) of the target model over a sequence of iterative queries `[Wang_2024_Advqdet]`. By systematically altering the input and observing the changes in the output confidence scores, the attacker can approximate the gradient landscape and iteratively guide the input toward a successful misclassification or malicious generation. While highly effective, these attacks require a massive number of queries to the target model, leaving a distinct behavioral footprint that defenders can potentially exploit. Furthermore, the rise of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has introduced new vectors for transferable adversarial examples. Recent research indicates that while traditional attacks focus on aligning global features (such as the `[CLS]` token in CLIP-based models), they often overlook the rich local information encoded in patch tokens, leading to suboptimal alignment and revealing new avenues for generating highly transferable adversarial examples `[Jia_2025_Adversarial]`.

## 2. Domain-Specific Vulnerabilities

As AI systems become increasingly specialized, adversarial attacks have evolved to exploit domain-specific vulnerabilities. The assumption that a defense mechanism effective in one domain (e.g., natural language processing) will seamlessly transfer to another (e.g., software engineering or computer vision) has been repeatedly challenged by empirical evidence. 

For instance, in the domain of software engineering, code pre-trained models have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across various code intelligence tasks, such as code completion, summarization, and vulnerability detection. However, these models exhibit unique vulnerabilities that differ significantly from those found in continuous data modalities like images. Adversarial attacks targeting code models often involve semantic-preserving transformations—such as variable renaming, dead code insertion, or structural refactoring—that do not alter the execution logic of the program but completely derail the model's predictive capabilities `[Yin_2025_LLM]`. Akin to traditional deep learning models, empirical studies reveal that these code-specific architectures are highly susceptible to carefully crafted adversarial examples, necessitating domain-aware robustness evaluations `[Yin_2025_LLM]`.

Similarly, in multimodal systems, the integration of text and visual inputs creates a complex attack surface where perturbations in one modality can force the model to ignore benign instructions in the other. Attackers can embed adversarial noise within an image that forces an MLLM to output malicious text, bypassing text-based safety filters entirely `[Jia_2025_Adversarial]`. Understanding these domain-specific nuances is critical for developing comprehensive threat models, as the definition of an "imperceptible perturbation" varies wildly depending on whether the input is a continuous image pixel, a discrete text token, or a functional line of code.

## 3. Healthcare AI Security: A Critical Frontier

Perhaps nowhere are the implications of domain-specific vulnerabilities more severe than in the healthcare sector. The integration of Large Language Models and advanced computer vision systems into healthcare applications offers promising advancements in medical diagnostics, treatment recommendations, and patient care automation. However, the susceptibility of these models to adversarial attacks poses a significant, life-threatening risk, potentially leading to harmful outcomes in delicate medical contexts `[Yang_2024_Adversarial]`.

In medical imaging, for example, adversarial noise that is entirely invisible to the human eye can alter the diagnosis of a benign tumor to malignant, or vice versa. When LLMs are utilized for clinical decision support, adversarial prompts—or slightly perturbed patient histories—can manipulate the model into recommending incorrect drug dosages or contraindicating necessary treatments. Recent studies have demonstrated adversarial attacking strategies that, despite their simplicity in implementation, possess the ability to significantly alter a model's operational behavior within specific healthcare tasks `[Yang_2024_Adversarial]`. 

The threat actors in this space are not limited to traditional hackers. Such techniques could potentially be exploited by a range of entities, including competitive pharmaceutical companies seeking to manipulate automated drug efficacy reviews, or malicious actors aiming to disrupt hospital operations `[Yang_2024_Adversarial]`. The deployment of custom and specialized LLMs in healthcare automation processes underscores the imperative for advanced security protocols. Standard adversarial training is often insufficient in this domain, as medical datasets are highly sensitive, heavily imbalanced, and difficult to augment without losing clinical validity. Consequently, safeguarding these technologies requires specialized, inference-time defense mechanisms that can ensure reliable use in critical sectors without compromising the model's diagnostic accuracy `[Yang_2024_Adversarial]`.

## 4. Defending the API: Stateful Detection

Given the limitations of adversarial training—which is computationally expensive and often degrades performance on clean data—researchers have increasingly turned to inference-time detection mechanisms. One of the most promising paradigms for defending against query-based black-box attacks is **Stateful Detection**.

Unlike stateless defenses that evaluate each input in isolation, stateful detection leverages the historical context of a user's interactions with the model. Because query-based attacks require the adversary to send hundreds or thousands of highly similar, iteratively perturbed inputs to estimate gradients, they generate a highly anomalous query trajectory. For a current query $x_t$, the task of a stateful detector is to determine whether there exists a historical query $x_k$ such that their similarity exceeds a certain threshold $\mu$ `[Wang_2024_Advqdet]`. If the similarity (often measured via $L_2$ distance or cosine similarity in a latent feature space) is abnormally high across a sequence of queries, the system flags the interaction as an ongoing attack and can block the user or return dummy logits to disrupt the gradient estimation.

However, implementing stateful detection in real-world, large-scale systems presents significant challenges. First, attackers can employ Sybil attacks, distributing their queries across multiple fake accounts or IP addresses to evade per-user stateful tracking. To counter this, advanced stateful detectors must compute the distance between the current query and historical queries from *all* users, which introduces massive computational overhead `[Wang_2024_Advqdet]`. Second, existing stateful detection methods historically suffer from a poor trade-off between the detection rate and the false positive rate (FPR). If the similarity threshold $\mu$ is set too low, the system will flag benign users who happen to upload similar images or ask similar questions; if set too high, adaptive attackers can bypass the detector by taking larger step sizes in their optimization process. Overcoming this trade-off requires a feature extractor that is exceptionally sensitive to adversarial trajectories while remaining invariant to benign semantic similarities.

## 5. Enhancing Robustness with Contrastive Prompt Tuning

To address the shortcomings of traditional stateful detection, recent advancements have leveraged self-supervised representation learning, specifically adapting it for adversarial robustness. A breakthrough in this area is the development of **Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning (ACPT)**, which serves as the foundation for state-of-the-art stateful detectors like AdvQDet `[Wang_2024_Advqdet]`.

Contrastive Learning (CL) is a powerful technique that pulls together the representations of similar samples (positive pairs) while pushing apart dissimilar ones (negative pairs). In the context of adversarial defense, ACPT adopts a two-stream contrastive prompt tuning paradigm designed to train robust feature extractors without requiring full model fine-tuning. The architecture utilizes a pre-trained vision-language model, such as the CLIP image encoder, and introduces learnable prompt tokens to adapt the model's latent space for attack detection `[Wang_2024_Advqdet]`.

The ACPT framework operates via two distinct streams:
1. **The Clean Stream:** This stream focuses on preserving the model's core semantic understanding. Two augmented views of a clean image form a Clean-to-Clean (C2C) pair. The objective here is to pull together the augmented versions of the same image, ensuring that benign variations (e.g., cropping, lighting changes) do not trigger false positives in the stateful detector `[Wang_2024_Advqdet]`.
2. **The Adversarial Stream:** This stream is explicitly designed to neutralize adversarial perturbations in the feature space. It utilizes contrastive losses to pull together the representations of a clean image and all of its adversarial counterparts generated under various data augmentations. By forcing the model to map an adversarial example to the exact same point in the latent space as its clean origin, the feature extractor becomes highly robust to adaptive attacks `[Wang_2024_Advqdet]`.

By fine-tuning the CLIP image encoder using this dual-stream approach, ACPT produces embeddings where the distance between iterative adversarial queries is minimized, making them easily detectable by a stateful system. Conversely, the distance between genuinely different benign queries is maintained. Although only fine-tuned on standard datasets like ImageNet, ACPT has demonstrated superb zero-shot capability, achieving state-of-the-art detection performance across a wide range of downstream tasks and datasets `[Wang_2024_Advqdet]`. 

When integrated into a stateful detection framework like AdvQDet, this contrastive prompt tuning approach effectively solves the historical trade-off between detection rate and false positives. It allows the system to maintain a high threshold for benign interactions while accurately identifying the clustered, iterative latent trajectories characteristic of query-based black-box attacks. This synergy between stateful historical tracking and contrastively tuned robust representations represents a critical step forward in securing AI APIs against inference-time exploitation.

inference_time_threats_adversarial_attac.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks
inference_time_threats_adversarial_attac.text:
**Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks**

The deployment of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including Large Language Models (LLMs), Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), and specialized code-generation models, has revolutionized numerous sectors. However, this widespread adoption has concurrently expanded the attack surface, introducing sophisticated inference-time threats. Unlike training-time vulnerabilities such as data poisoning, inference-time threats exploit the operational phase of a deployed model. Adversarial attacks, a prominent category of these threats, involve the subtle manipulation of input data to deceive the model into producing incorrect, unintended, or malicious outputs. While early research predominantly focused on imperceptible perturbations in image classification tasks, the landscape has evolved dramatically. Modern adversarial attacks are increasingly complex, targeting the intricate architectures of transformer-based models and exploiting domain-specific vulnerabilities across diverse applications, from healthcare diagnostics to software engineering. This section delves into the multifaceted nature of inference-time adversarial attacks, exploring domain-specific vulnerabilities, the critical exploitation of healthcare systems using datasets like MIMIC-III, the mechanics of black-box query attacks, the offensive weaponization of AI capabilities, and the architectural defenses being developed to mitigate these pervasive threats.

**Domain-Specific Vulnerabilities**

As AI models become increasingly specialized, they inherit and introduce domain-specific vulnerabilities that adversaries can exploit. The architectural nuances and the nature of the data processed by these models create unique attack vectors that differ significantly from general-purpose models. In the realm of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), which integrate vision and language capabilities, the alignment between different modalities presents a critical vulnerability. MLLMs remain highly susceptible to transferable adversarial examples, where an attack crafted on a surrogate model successfully deceives an unseen target model [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. Traditional methods for generating these targeted attacks typically focus on aligning global features, such as the [CLS] token in Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models, between the adversarial sample and the target sample. However, this approach often overlooks the rich, fine-grained local information encoded within individual patch tokens [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. This oversight leads to suboptimal alignment and limits the transferability of the attacks. To exploit this vulnerability more effectively, sophisticated frameworks like FOA-Attack have been proposed. FOA-Attack is a targeted transferable adversarial attack framework that jointly aligns both global and local features, thereby significantly improving transferability against both open-source and closed-source MLLMs [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. By incorporating a global cosine similarity loss alongside a local clustering optimal transport loss and a dynamic ensemble weighting strategy, such attacks demonstrate the fragility of multimodal alignment mechanisms [Jia_2025_Adversarial].

Similarly, in the domain of software engineering, code pre-trained models have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance across various code intelligence tasks. These models, typically instantiated as transformer-based autoregressive models trained to predict the next token in a sequence of code [Thang_2026_LLM], are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, empirical studies reveal that, akin to traditional deep learning models, these code-specific LLMs are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks [Yin_2025_LLM]. Adversaries can introduce subtle, semantically preserving perturbations into the source code—such as renaming variables, inserting dead code, or altering syntactic structures—that cause the model to fail in tasks like code summarization, vulnerability detection, or code generation. The deterministic and highly structured nature of programming languages means that even minor adversarial modifications can have cascading effects on the model's output, highlighting a critical domain-specific vulnerability that must be addressed to ensure the secure deployment of AI in software development pipelines [Yin_2025_LLM].

**Healthcare/MIMIC-III Exploitation**

The integration of LLMs into healthcare applications offers promising advancements in medical diagnostics, treatment recommendations, and patient care management. However, the susceptibility of these models to adversarial attacks poses a severe and immediate threat, potentially leading to catastrophic outcomes in delicate medical contexts where precision and reliability are paramount [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. The exploitation of healthcare-specific AI systems underscores the critical need for robust evaluation methodologies.

Recent studies have rigorously investigated the vulnerability of state-of-the-art models, such as GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4, within representative healthcare tasks. To simulate realistic clinical scenarios, researchers frequently utilize the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) dataset, a large, publicly available database containing de-identified health data from over 40,000 patients admitted to critical care units [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. In a comprehensive evaluation, researchers extracted a subset of 1,200 extensive discharge notes from the MIMIC-III dataset to serve as complex, real-world inputs for LLMs [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. The objective was to explore the models' susceptibility to adversarial attacks across critical tasks, including vaccination guidance and medication prescription [Yang_2024_Adversarial].

Under normal, unperturbed conditions, the baseline results generated by advanced models like GPT-4 generally align well with the actual clinical statistics and ground truth present in the MIMIC-III data, demonstrating their potential utility in clinical decision support [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. However, the introduction of prompt-based adversarial attacks reveals a stark fragility. When subjected to these attacks, the models exhibit significant deviations in their outputs, resulting in a substantial decline in accuracy and reliability [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. These adversarial prompts are designed to subtly manipulate the context or the phrasing of the medical inquiry without altering the underlying clinical facts, yet they successfully deceive the model into providing incorrect medical advice or inappropriate medication recommendations. The feasibility of replicating these attacks in complex medical environments, beyond simplified single-trigger word experiments, highlights a profound vulnerability [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. The exploitation of MIMIC-III data demonstrates that adversaries do not need to alter the patient's physiological data; merely manipulating the interaction interface or the prompt structure is sufficient to compromise the integrity of the AI-driven healthcare system. This vulnerability necessitates urgent attention, as the deployment of unhardened LLMs in clinical settings could directly jeopardize patient safety.

**Black-Box Query Attacks**

In many real-world deployment scenarios, the internal architecture, weights, and training data of a target AI model are proprietary and inaccessible to external users. This necessitates the use of black-box threat models, where the adversary can only interact with the system by submitting inputs (queries) and observing the corresponding outputs [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. Despite this restricted access, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) and LLMs remain highly vulnerable to query-based black-box adversarial attacks [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

Query-based black-box attacks operate by systematically estimating the adversarial gradients required to craft a successful perturbation. Since the adversary cannot compute the gradients directly via backpropagation, they rely on the information returned by the target model—typically probability vectors or confidence scores—over a sequence of carefully designed queries [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. During this iterative process, the attacker submits an initial input, observes the model's confidence scores across different classes or tokens, and uses this feedback to approximate the gradient of the loss function. The input is then incrementally perturbed in the direction that maximizes the error of the target model. This cycle of querying and updating continues until the adversarial example successfully crosses the decision boundary, causing a misclassification or an unintended generation [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

The efficacy of these attacks lies in their ability to optimize adversarial examples iteratively without requiring white-box access. However, this iterative optimization process inherently requires the adversary to launch multiple, often visually or semantically similar queries to the target model [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. For instance, in image classification, the sequence of queried images will exhibit only minute variations as the perturbation is gradually refined. In natural language processing, the queries might involve slight lexical substitutions or syntactic rephrasings. While these attacks are highly effective at bypassing standard defenses, the distinct pattern of repetitive, highly correlated queries generated during the gradient estimation phase presents a detectable signature that defenders can exploit.

**Offensive Weaponization**

The sophisticated capabilities of modern AI models, particularly LLMs trained on vast repositories of code and technical documentation, have inadvertently facilitated the offensive weaponization of AI. Adversarial attacks are no longer confined to academic exercises demonstrating model fragility; they are increasingly being leveraged to develop tangible cyber threats and exploit real-world vulnerabilities. This dual-use nature of AI presents a significant challenge for cybersecurity professionals.

Adversaries can weaponize AI models to accelerate exploit development and automate the discovery of vulnerabilities in software and hardware systems. For example, LLMs can be manipulated through adversarial prompting to generate malicious code, craft sophisticated phishing campaigns, or identify weaknesses in firmware updates [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. By bypassing the ethical guardrails and safety filters embedded within these models, attackers can extract actionable intelligence on common vulnerabilities, such as improper input validation (CWE-20) or uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400) [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. Furthermore, the weaponization extends to hardware exploitation. Adversarial interactions with AI models can yield detailed methodologies for conducting complex hardware attacks, such as voltage glitching [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. Voltage glitching involves intentionally introducing fluctuations in the power supply of a device to induce faults, bypass security checks, and potentially gain unauthorized access to the system [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. The ability of AI models to synthesize information on tools like `binwalk` for firmware analysis or to guide the identification of vulnerable devices using search engines like Shodan significantly lowers the barrier to entry for malicious actors [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. This offensive weaponization transforms AI from a defensive asset into a potent tool for conducting malicious cyberactivity, necessitating the development of robust countermeasures to prevent the misuse of these powerful technologies.

**Architectural Defenses**

To mitigate the escalating threat of inference-time adversarial attacks, researchers are developing sophisticated architectural defenses that aim to harden models and detect malicious activity. These defenses operate at various levels, from modifying the underlying model architecture to implementing external monitoring frameworks.

One promising approach to countering query-box black-box attacks is the deployment of stateful detection frameworks [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. Recognizing that query-based attacks inherently require the submission of multiple, highly similar queries to estimate gradients, defenders can implement systems that monitor the query history of individual users or IP addresses. A stateful detection framework leverages a robust feature extractor, such as a pre-trained image encoder or a sentence transformer, to analyze incoming queries [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. By computing the similarity between the current query and previously submitted queries, the framework can identify the repetitive patterns characteristic of iterative adversarial optimization. If the similarity exceeds a predefined threshold, indicating a potential attack, the system can block the user, return randomized outputs to disrupt the gradient estimation, or alert administrators [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

In the domain of code generation, where models are vulnerable to input perturbations, architectural defenses often incorporate adversarial training methodologies. To address the real-world scenario where LLM-generated code may undergo minor adversarial modifications, frameworks like CodeGPTSensor+ have been proposed [Yin_2025_LLM]. This enhanced system employs adversarial training to significantly improve the model's robustness against input perturbations [Yin_2025_LLM]. The defense integrates a multi-objective optimization-based adversarial sample generation module, which systematically creates diverse and challenging adversarial examples during the training phase. By exposing the model to these adversarial samples and penalizing incorrect predictions, the model learns to extract more robust features and becomes less sensitive to semantically preserving modifications [Yin_2025_LLM].

Furthermore, the development of comprehensive benchmarks is crucial for evaluating the efficacy of architectural defenses. As LLMs become increasingly capable of generating functional source code, detecting AI-generated code—especially when it has been written or modified in an adversarial manner—becomes critical for accountability and security [Orel_2026_AI]. Existing datasets are often narrow, focusing on simple binary classification under in-distribution settings. To overcome these limitations, large-scale benchmarks like AICD Bench systematically evaluate detectors across multiple axes of variation, including different generator families, programming languages, and adversarial modifications [Orel_2026_AI]. By rigorously testing architectural defenses against a wide array of adversarial scenarios, researchers can identify vulnerabilities and develop more resilient AI systems capable of withstanding the complex inference-time threats of the future.

inference_time_threats_prompt_injection.text:
## 5. Inference-Time Threats: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking

### 5.1 The 2025-2026 Paradigm Shift in Adversarial Optimization

The research landscape of Large Language Model (LLM) security, specifically concerning prompt injection and jailbreak attacks, underwent a rapid and transformative evolution between 2025 and 2026. This period is characterized by a definitive shift from static, rule-based, and single-model defensive paradigms toward a highly dynamic, automated, and co-evolutionary adversarial arms race [l2_Prompt Injection_v100]. In the early phases of 2025, the literature reflected a growing consensus that static defenses were fundamentally inadequate against sophisticated adversaries. Researchers demonstrated that existing guardrails could be consistently bypassed by employing adaptive optimization techniques. During this phase, the offensive state-of-the-art advanced significantly through the application of modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms. Together, these automated methodologies achieved alarming Attack Success Rates (ASR) ranging from 50% to 71% against state-of-the-art LLM agents [Zhan_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_LLM, Maloyan_2025_LLM]. This established a baseline understanding that attackers were successfully automating the discovery of adversarial prompts in both black-box and agentic environments, forcing the defensive community to fundamentally rethink alignment and moderation strategies.

### 5.2 Adaptive White-Box and Black-Box Optimization

The automation of jailbreaking heavily relied on adapting established gradient-based and search-based optimization techniques to target specific defensive mechanisms. In 2025, researchers conducted the first comprehensive evaluation of existing Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) defenses against adaptive attacks in LLM agents [Zhan_2025_LLM]. In an IPI attack, an adversary embeds malicious instructions into external data sources, which the LLM agent subsequently retrieves and processes. Assuming white-box access, attackers inserted optimized adversarial strings—either as prefixes or suffixes—into the external content. The core optimization relied on the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) algorithm, which was adapted to maximize the probability of the LLM generating a specific target response, such as a ReAct thought process or a JSON function call that executes an attacker-controlled tool [Zhan_2025_LLM]. 

To systematically bypass specific guardrails, specialized variants of GCG were introduced. Multi-objective GCG (M-GCG) added a stealth objective to evade detection-based defenses by jointly or iteratively optimizing the adversarial string to be misclassified as benign. Two-stage GCG (T-GCG) specifically targeted paraphrasing defenses by training a two-part string where the paraphraser's output matched the target trigger. Furthermore, AutoDAN was utilized to generate semantically meaningful adversarial strings designed to bypass Perplexity Filtering (PF). Through these adaptive attack strategies, eight different state-of-the-art defenses were consistently bypassed, achieving an ASR of over 50% and highlighting the critical necessity of incorporating adaptive attack evaluations when designing LLM agent defenses [Zhan_2025_LLM].

Parallel to gradient-based methods, search-based optimization demonstrated profound efficacy, particularly against LLM-as-a-judge systems. These systems, increasingly used for evaluating text quality and code correctness, proved highly vulnerable to prompt injection [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Researchers developed a comprehensive framework for adversarial attacks against LLM judges, distinguishing between content-author attacks (where malicious text is submitted for evaluation) and system-prompt attacks (where the evaluation template itself is compromised). Building upon the HOUYI approach, the attack framework utilized three core components: a Framework Component to establish contextual relevance, a Separator Component to induce cognitive overload via complex word bombardment and pattern disruption, and a Disruptor Component for direct command injection and context nullification [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. 

Within this framework, the Adaptive Search-Based Attack (ASA) was introduced, leveraging genetic algorithms to optimize attack strings based purely on model feedback. Large-scale comparative evaluations across five models—including frontier models like GPT-4 and Claude-3-Opus, as well as open-source models like Gemma-3-27B-Instruct—demonstrated that sophisticated attacks could achieve success rates up to 73.8%. Notably, smaller models such as Gemma-3-4B-Instruct exhibited higher vulnerability, with a 65.9% average success rate, and attacks showed high transferability (50.5% to 62.6%) across different architectures. The study provided quantitative evidence that employing multi-model committees with diverse architectures could reduce attack success rates by 20 to 47 percentage points [Maloyan_2025_LLM].

### 5.3 Agentic Vulnerabilities and MCTS Fuzzing

As LLMs evolved into autonomous agents capable of interacting with complex environments and external tools, the attack surface expanded significantly. The black-box nature of real-world commercial agents, combined with their architectural complexity and the diversity of user tasks they manage, presented unique challenges for systematic security assessment [Wang_2025_LLM]. To address this, researchers proposed AGENTVIGIL, the first generic, automated black-box fuzzing framework explicitly designed to discover and exploit indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities in LLM agents [Wang_2025_LLM].

AGENTVIGIL operates by injecting malicious instructions into the external data sources that a target agent interacts with, aiming to fool the agent into executing the attacker's chosen task instead of the original user task. The fuzzing pipeline begins with a curated initial corpus of adversarial prompt templates that incorporate role-playing, delimiter-based, and obfuscation strategies, complete with placeholders for dynamic adaptation. These seeds enter an iterative fuzzing loop governed by a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) based seed selector. The selector utilizes the Upper Confidence Bound 1 (UCB1) algorithm to optimally balance the exploration of new prompt variants against the exploitation of historically high-scoring seeds [Wang_2025_LLM].

Because the target agent operates as a black box, the framework relies on sparse, binary feedback—specifically, the success or failure of the injection task. To maximize this weak signal, AGENTVIGIL employs an adaptive seed scoring strategy that calculates a final score based on a hybrid metric combining the ASR with attack coverage. A helper LLM (such as GPT-4o-mini) acts as a mutator, applying one of five basic mutation strategies: Shorten, Expand, Rephrase, Crossover, or GenerateSimilar. Empirical evaluations on public benchmarks, including AgentDojo and VWA-adv, demonstrated that AGENTVIGIL achieved high attack success rates of 70% to 71% against agents powered by frontier models like o3-mini, GPT-4o, and Gemini. Furthermore, the framework validated the practical applicability of these attacks in real-world environments by successfully misleading a web agent to navigate to arbitrary and malicious URLs [Wang_2025_LLM].

### 5.4 The Bifurcation of Offensive Research: Efficiency vs. Complexity

As 2025 progressed, the temporal trend in offensive LLM security bifurcated into two distinct but interconnected trajectories: the development of dynamic, ensemble-based attack systems (as seen in AGENTVIGIL and ASA) and the pursuit of extreme computational efficiency [l2_Prompt Injection_v100]. On the efficiency front, a critical turning point was the introduction of knowledge distillation to transfer jailbreaking capabilities from massive, high-capacity LLMs to highly efficient Small Language Models (SLMs) [Slms_2025_Efficient]. 

This asymmetric warfare tactic was formalized through the Adversarial Prompt Distillation (APD) framework. The APD methodology consists of a multi-stage approach to transfer capabilities from a teacher LLM (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B) to a lightweight student SLM (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa). First, the teacher model is pre-trained on a dataset constructed via the Cartesian product of harmful instructions and selected templates, optimized using Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss to maximize the likelihood of generating harmful outputs. Next, the teacher's adversarial capabilities are distilled into the SLM by aligning their output distributions using KL divergence loss. To handle vocabulary mismatches, projection layers map logits to a shared dimension, while the last four layers of the student model are fine-tuned using masked language modeling to enhance diversity [Slms_2025_Efficient].

Finally, a Reinforcement Learning Optimization (RLAIF) phase employs a Policy Gradient method to maximize a composite reward function that balances stealthiness, harmfulness, and diversity, incorporating dynamic temperature control to prevent mode collapse. This distillation process allowed attackers to generate adversarial inputs 3.7 times faster than traditional LLM-based attacks while maintaining an exceptionally high ASR of over 96%, significantly reducing the memory demands and generation time required to execute state-of-the-art jailbreaks [Slms_2025_Efficient].

### 5.5 Co-Evolutionary Defenses and Real-Time Mitigation

Consequently, the defensive community was forced to pivot away from computationally heavy, static guardrails toward adaptive, real-time mitigation strategies. One prominent solution introduced in 2025 was AEGIS, an Automated co-Evolutionary framework for Guarding prompt Injections Schema [Liu_2025_Aegis]. AEGIS systematically evolves both attackers and defenders to provide adaptive robustness without requiring manual prompt engineering or model fine-tuning. The framework operates via a GAN-inspired, two-level optimization process. In the outer loop, an Attacker module and a Defender module alternate turns; the attacker generates adversarial prompts to maximize ASR, while the defender generates prompts to maximize True Positive Rate (TPR) and True Negative Rate (TNR) [Liu_2025_Aegis].

In the inner loop, AEGIS utilizes TGO+, an enhanced textual gradient optimization module tailored for black-box LLMs. TGO+ simulates gradient-like updates using natural language feedback. It features two key innovations: 'Multi-Route Gradient Optimization', which generates textual gradients based on multiple optimization metrics simultaneously, and a 'Gradient Buffer', which stores past textual gradients to encourage the exploration of novel pathways and prevent cyclical optimization. Evaluated on a real-world automated assignment grading application, AEGIS consistently outperformed existing baselines, improving the TPR by 0.20 compared to previous state-of-the-art methods, with only a marginal 0.02 decrease in TNR. Ablation studies confirmed that co-evolution, gradient replay, and multi-objective optimization are critical for sustaining long-term robustness [Liu_2025_Aegis].

Simultaneously, researchers developed lightweight moderation architectures to ensure LLM alignment without degrading model responses to benign prompts or introducing significant barriers to scalable implementation. The Real-Time Self-Tuning (RTST) framework exemplifies this approach [Zhang_2025_Real]. RTST is a multi-agent moderator framework that relies on a 'Behavior Set'—a human-readable JSON list of criteria describing prompts, each assigned a base score and a tunable weight. When a user submits a prompt, the Main Model and an 'Evaluator' agent are queried in parallel. The Evaluator matches the prompt to K Behaviors and calculates a total score. Depending on whether the score meets a specific threshold, either a 'False Negative Reviewer' or a 'False Positive Reviewer' agent evaluates the analysis. The Reviewer makes the final safety determination and can self-tune the system in real-time by suggesting weight adjustments or adding new adversarial Behaviors to the set, demonstrating significant improvements in ASR and F1 scores against modern jailbreaks compared to traditional fine-tuning or classifier models [Zhang_2025_Real].

### 5.6 System Prompt Strategies and the Think Mode Paradox

Beyond external moderation frameworks, the intrinsic interaction between system prompts and in-context learning emerged as a critical factor in LLM vulnerability. In 2026, researchers conducted the first systematic study of interaction effects between few-shot demonstrations and system prompt strategies for LLM safety [Wang_2026_LLM]. The study evaluated two primary prompt-based defenses: Role-Oriented Prompts (RoP), which frame the LLM as a safe AI assistant, and Task-Oriented Prompts (ToP), which explicitly define safe response generation as the task objective.

The investigation revealed a divergent interaction effect: few-shot demonstrations enhance RoP by up to 4.5% but degrade ToP by up to 21.2%. To explain these phenomena, researchers developed a mathematical framework. For RoP, Bayesian in-context learning models 'role reinforcement', where few-shot examples act as likelihood evidence that strengthens the posterior probability of safe latent concepts. Conversely, for ToP, attention analysis—incorporating softmax attention entropy, the 'lost in the middle' position bias, and the 'attention sink' phenomenon—models 'attention dilution'. Prepending few-shot examples pushes task instructions into middle context positions, thereby diluting the model's attention on the core safety directives [Wang_2026_LLM].

Furthermore, the study identified the 'think mode paradox', revealing that reasoning-enhanced models exhibit consistently higher vulnerability to both jailbreak attacks and negative few-shot interactions. Based on these findings, practical deployment recommendations advise the use of RoP combined with few-shot examples for optimal safety, while strictly avoiding the combination of ToP with few-shot demonstrations [Wang_2026_LLM]. This nuanced understanding of prompt interactions underscores the complexity of inference-time threats, demonstrating that even well-intentioned defensive configurations can inadvertently expand the attack surface if the underlying attention and learning mechanisms are not properly accounted for.

integrity_and_factual_consistency_halluc.title: 6. Model Integrity and Reliability: Hallucinations
integrity_and_factual_consistency_halluc.text:
## 6. Model Integrity and Reliability: Hallucinations

The generation of non-factual, unsubstantiated, or logically inconsistent information—commonly referred to as hallucination—remains a primary obstacle to the reliable deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) [Liu_2025_Attention]. Between 2023 and 2026, the research landscape surrounding LLM hallucinations and factual consistency underwent a rapid and sophisticated evolution [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v2]. This trajectory reflects a fundamental shift from basic, computationally expensive detection mechanisms toward highly optimized, mechanistically informed, and conceptually nuanced frameworks [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v2]. Early approaches primarily treated hallucinations as binary errors and relied heavily on brute-force LLM-as-evaluator paradigms. However, as the field matured, researchers began to explore the internal representations of models, redefining the nature of non-factual generation and developing targeted mitigation strategies that operate at the level of attention mechanisms and reasoning trajectories.

### 6.1 The Early Phase (2023): Establishing the LLM-as-Evaluator Paradigm

In the initial phase of widespread LLM deployment circa 2023, the field was characterized by an urgent need to establish baseline detection methodologies [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v2]. A dominant approach during this period involved leveraging the LLMs themselves as evaluators to police their own outputs. A landmark development in this era was the introduction of ChainPoll, a novel, efficient, and explainable hallucination detection methodology that utilized detailed Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [Friel_2023_LLM]. ChainPoll treated hallucination detection as a binary classification problem, prompting an evaluator model (such as gpt-3.5-turbo) to judge whether a given completion contained inaccuracies [Friel_2023_LLM]. 

To ensure reliability and cost-efficiency, ChainPoll employed a carefully engineered "detailed CoT" prompt to elicit systematic explanations alongside boolean judgments, running the process multiple times (typically five) using batch inference [Friel_2023_LLM]. The final hallucination score was calculated by dividing the number of affirmative hallucination judgments by the total number of runs [Friel_2023_LLM]. This approach dramatically outperformed existing metrics like G-Eval, SelfCheckGPT, and GPTScore [Friel_2023_LLM]. To validate this methodology, researchers developed RealHall, a curated suite of challenging benchmark datasets including COVID-QA, DROP, Open Assistant, and TriviaQA [Friel_2023_LLM]. On the RealHall benchmark, ChainPoll achieved an aggregate AUROC of 0.781, surpassing the next best theoretical algorithm by 11% while utilizing only a quarter of the inference cost [Friel_2023_LLM]. Furthermore, ChainPoll introduced two specific metrics: Adherence, designed for closed-domain Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) workflows, and Correctness, focused on open-domain logical mistakes [Friel_2023_LLM]. Crucially, the CoT text generated during the evaluation process could be reused to provide human-readable justifications, establishing a foundational paradigm for explainable, self-policing models [Friel_2023_LLM].

### 6.2 Conceptual Maturation (2024): Beyond Binary Errors

Moving into 2024, the field experienced a significant conceptual maturation, recognizing that treating all non-factual generations as strict database errors was overly simplistic [l2_LLM Hallucinations_v2]. This theoretical pivot was exemplified by research that proposed redefining LLM hallucinations as "confabulations" [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. Drawing on cognitive science and narrative theory, researchers argued that confabulations should not be viewed categorically as negative pitfalls, but rather as manifestations of a latent narrative impulse to generate substantive and coherent outputs when factual information is lacking [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. Empirical evaluations using an ELECTRA-large encoder-only model on dialogic benchmarks (such as FaithDial and HaluEval) demonstrated that hallucinated outputs exhibited significantly higher levels of narrativity compared to factual outputs [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. Furthermore, statistical analyses using beta regression revealed a significant positive correlation between narrativity and semantic coherence, suggesting that the tendency for LLMs to confabulate is intimately associated with their positive capacity for coherent text generation [Sui_2024_Confabulation].

Concurrently, the demand for scalable oversight led to the development of more sophisticated annotation and detection frameworks. In 2024, researchers introduced an iterative self-training framework based on the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to simultaneously scale up hallucination annotation datasets and improve annotator accuracy [Gu_2024_Anah]. This framework utilized a phased, multi-turn dialogue annotation process comprising Factual Existence Judgment, Reference Information Extraction, and Hallucination-Type Judgment, aligning closely with human cognitive processes [Gu_2024_Anah]. During the E-Step, the annotator estimated ground-truth annotations using a self-consistency strategy with 32 independent outputs, selecting the most representative sample via majority voting [Gu_2024_Anah]. In the M-Step, model parameters were updated using the newly scaled data [Gu_2024_Anah]. This progressive scaling strategy culminated in the release of ANAH-v2, a 7-billion parameter hallucination annotator that surpassed GPT-4 in accuracy [Gu_2024_Anah]. ANAH-v2 achieved state-of-the-art zero-shot detection results on HaluEval (81.54%) and HalluQA (94.44%), and demonstrated practical utility in mitigation; by employing a simple re-ranking strategy guided by the annotator, the Natural Language Inference (NLI) metric for LLM generations on HaluEval increased from 25% to 37% [Gu_2024_Anah].

### 6.3 Mechanistic Interpretability and Internal States (2025)

By 2025, the focus of hallucination research shifted decisively toward mechanistic interpretability, aiming to detect and prevent non-factual generation by analyzing the model's internal states and attention mechanisms. Traditional consistency-based approaches, which relied on stochastically generating multiple responses to measure output variance, were computationally expensive [Liu_2025_Attention]. To address this, researchers proposed Attention-Guided SElf-Reflection (AGSER), a novel zero-shot hallucination detection approach that leveraged internal attention contributions [Liu_2025_Attention]. AGSER operated by calculating token contribution scores based on the mean value of attention across all self-attention layers from each token to the last token of the query [Liu_2025_Attention]. The input query was then split into an "attentive query" (comprising the top tokens with the highest contribution scores) and a "non-attentive query" [Liu_2025_Attention]. 

The core insight of AGSER was that attentive and non-attentive segments exhibit distinct consistency behaviors during factual versus hallucinated generation [Liu_2025_Attention]. Both queries were fed separately into the LLM, and Rouge-L consistency scores were calculated between the new responses and the original answer [Liu_2025_Attention]. The final hallucination estimator was computed by subtracting the non-attentive consistency score from the attentive consistency score; a lower final score indicated a higher probability of hallucination [Liu_2025_Attention]. AGSER significantly reduced computational overhead, requiring only three LLM passes and two sets of tokens, while achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot detection performance across multiple popular LLMs [Liu_2025_Attention].

Parallel advancements in 2025 focused on Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) as a framework for assessing the reliability of model outputs. Researchers designed pre-trained UQ heads—supervised auxiliary Transformer modules attached to frozen LLMs—that significantly outperformed classical unsupervised techniques for claim-level hallucination detection [Shelmanov_2025_LLM]. Instead of relying on hidden states, which are prone to overfitting, these UQ heads extracted features primarily from the LLM's attention maps and the logarithms of top-m token probabilities [Shelmanov_2025_LLM]. The architecture utilized a feature size reduction network, a multi-layer transformer encoder, and a two-layer classification neural network with GELU activations and dropout [Shelmanov_2025_LLM]. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrated that these plug-and-play modules, developed for models like the Llama series, Gemma 2, and Mistral, generalized robustly across out-of-domain topics and cross-lingual settings (including Russian, Chinese, and German) despite being trained exclusively on English data [Shelmanov_2025_LLM].

### 6.4 Factual Consistency and Contextual Nuance (2025)

As detection mechanisms became more sophisticated, researchers also began to explore how factual consistency varied across different contexts and user interactions. In 2025, the introduction of ConsistencyAI provided an independent, scalable benchmark to measure whether LLMs altered their factual claims based on the demographic or ideological persona of the user [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. The framework queried LLMs with identical prompts requesting facts and sources, but prepended different persona descriptions [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. Using a BERT Sentence Transformer (SBERT) to generate sentence-level embeddings, the system computed cross-persona cosine similarity to quantify factual overlap [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. Evaluating 19 leading LLMs across 15 topics and 100 diverse personas, the study established a baseline mean factual consistency score of 0.8656, revealing that consistency dropped significantly on controversial or dynamic topics (e.g., the Israeli-Palestinian conflict) and identifying non-random refusal patterns where models disproportionately failed to respond to specific personas [Banyas_2025_LLMs].

Similarly, domain-specific evaluations revealed critical vulnerabilities that general metrics often missed. In the context of text-based explainable recommenders, researchers identified a severe "factuality gap" where high semantic similarity scores masked high hallucination rates [Kabongo_2025_Factual]. To address this, they introduced a prompting-based pipeline using Llama-3-8B-Instruct to extract atomic explanatory statements from user reviews, constructing factual ground-truth explanations [Kabongo_2025_Factual]. By evaluating generated explanations against this ground truth using novel statement-level alignment metrics that combined LLM-based and Natural Language Inference (NLI)-based approaches, the study provided a fine-grained assessment of factual consistency, highlighting the limitations of traditional evaluation paradigms [Kabongo_2025_Factual].

### 6.5 Advanced Mitigation and Process Supervision (2026)

The culmination of this research trajectory is evident in the advanced mitigation strategies developed by 2026, which moved beyond post-hoc detection toward proactive intervention during the reasoning process itself. A notable advancement was the introduction of a framework for constructing step-level supervision of CoT reasoning traces using information-theoretic labeling [Royer_2026_Process]. By generating structured reasoning outputs and validating final answers with task-specific functions, researchers defined a Monte Carlo Net Information Gain metric to obtain fine-grained labels that distinguished correct from incorrect reasoning steps [Royer_2026_Process]. These labels were subsequently used to train a highly competitive Process Reward Model [Royer_2026_Process]. Evaluations across diverse benchmarks, including mathematics, code generation, and text-to-SQL tasks, demonstrated that this step-level supervision enabled more effective selection of reasoning trajectories in a best-of-K setting [Royer_2026_Process]. This approach highlighted the potential of information-based labeling to provide richer supervision signals at a limited cost, marking a significant step toward building intrinsically reliable and trustworthy large language models [Royer_2026_Process].

model_reliability_hallucinations.title: 6. Model Reliability and Factual Consistency: LLM Hallucinations
model_reliability_hallucinations.text:
# 6. Model Reliability and Factual Consistency: LLM Hallucinations

The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has unlocked unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding, generation, and complex reasoning. However, the deployment of these models in high-stakes, real-world applications—such as healthcare diagnostics, legal analysis, and financial forecasting—remains fundamentally bottlenecked by the persistent challenge of "hallucinations." In the context of LLMs, hallucinations refer to instances where a model generates information that is syntactically plausible and delivered with high confidence, yet is factually incorrect, nonsensical, or entirely ungrounded in the provided source material. Ensuring model reliability and factual consistency has therefore emerged as a paramount objective within the artificial intelligence research community. The landscape of hallucination research has undergone a significant evolution, transitioning from basic, computationally expensive detection mechanisms to highly sophisticated, mechanistic, and persona-aware frameworks. This section explores the multifaceted domain of LLM hallucinations, tracing the trajectory from foundational detection methodologies and the advent of the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm, to state-of-the-art evaluation metrics like ChainPoll. Furthermore, we examine the critical nuances of factual consistency across diverse topics and user personas, and delve into emerging mechanistic frameworks that seek to understand, isolate, and control the internal representations driving these hallucinatory phenomena.

Historically, the detection of hallucinations relied heavily on traditional natural language generation (NLG) metrics, such as ROUGE, BLEU, or BERTScore. While useful for assessing general text similarity, these metrics primarily measure n-gram overlap or surface-level semantic similarity, making them fundamentally ill-equipped to capture the subtle semantic deviations and logical inconsistencies that characterize LLM hallucinations. As language models grew more capable, the research community recognized that the most effective tool for evaluating complex text was often another language model. This realization catalyzed the widespread adoption of the "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm. In this approach, a powerful, instruction-tuned LLM is prompted to act as an impartial evaluator, assessing the factuality of a target model's response against a given context or a set of established facts. The LLM-as-a-Judge framework offers a significant leap in evaluative nuance, as it can parse complex reasoning chains and identify subtle contradictions that traditional metrics miss. However, this paradigm introduces its own set of challenges, primarily concerning the scalability of high-quality annotations, the computational cost of querying massive judge models, and the inherent biases or blind spots of the judge itself.

To address the limitations of the standard LLM-as-a-Judge approach, recent advancements have focused on automating and scaling the oversight process through sophisticated training regimens. A notable contribution in this space is the work by Gu et al., who proposed an iterative self-training framework designed to simultaneously scale up hallucination datasets and enhance the accuracy of the hallucination annotator [Gu_2024_Anah]. Recognizing that manual annotation of hallucinations is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, their multi-iteration framework leverages an analytical, sentence-by-sentence annotation strategy. Crucially, this approach is theoretically grounded in the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, allowing the system to iteratively refine its understanding of hallucinatory patterns [Gu_2024_Anah]. During this process, the model alternates between generating annotations for unlabelled data and updating its own parameters based on the most confident predictions. Despite the progressive scaling and the increasing accuracy of the hallucination annotator achieved through this method, the authors acknowledge that a non-negligible margin of error may still persist [Gu_2024_Anah]. This highlights the inherent difficulty of the task and underscores the ongoing need for robust, multi-layered oversight mechanisms in automated hallucination detection.

A significant breakthrough in operationalizing and optimizing the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm is the development of ChainPoll, a novel methodology that substantially improves both the accuracy and efficiency of hallucination detection [Friel_2023_LLM]. Traditional detection metrics often struggle to balance computational overhead with evaluative precision; for instance, methods like SelfCheck-BertScore require sampling multiple full-length responses from the target model, which is highly resource-intensive. ChainPoll elegantly circumvents this inefficiency by employing a meticulously engineered, detailed Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt directed at a judge model, such as GPT-3.5-Turbo [Friel_2023_LLM]. The core mechanism involves asking the judge whether a specific completion contains hallucinations, forcing the model to articulate its reasoning step-by-step before arriving at a conclusion. To mitigate the variance inherent in LLM sampling, ChainPoll repeats this querying process multiple times—typically five—using batch inference for speed, and aggregates the results through a polling mechanism [Friel_2023_LLM]. This combination of detailed CoT and ensemble polling allows ChainPoll to outperform all other existing methods by a massive margin across a diverse range of benchmark tasks, establishing a new state-of-the-art [Friel_2023_LLM]. Furthermore, to ensure these metrics translate effectively to practical applications, Friel and colleagues developed RealHall, a curated suite of four challenging datasets designed to close the gap between academic evaluation and real-world LLM usage, giving researchers confidence that ChainPoll's superior performance will generalize to production environments [Friel_2023_LLM].

Beyond binary hallucination detection, a critical and highly nuanced dimension of model reliability is "factual consistency." Factual consistency refers to the degree to which an LLM maintains a stable, non-contradictory set of objective truths across different interactions, contexts, or when prompted to adopt different user personas. Measuring factual consistency does not necessarily require verifying the absolute truth of the claims against an external database; rather, by comparing the facts presented to different personas, researchers can assess the model's reliability, its truth-seeking tendency, and its vulnerability to sycophancy [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. Recent empirical studies have revealed that an LLM's factual consistency is highly variable and deeply sensitive to the topic of discourse. Banyas et al. conducted an extensive evaluation demonstrating that contemporary and controversial issues often yield significantly less reliable responses [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. For example, their analysis revealed that discussions surrounding the "job market" exhibited the lowest mean factual consistency score (0.07865), which was substantially lower than other topics [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. Interestingly, performance varies considerably across different model providers. In the context of the "vaccines" topic, xAI's models performed exceptionally well, with Grok-3 and Grok-4 achieving the two highest factual consistency scores, outperforming their own average scores across all other topics [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. This variance underscores that factual consistency is not a static attribute but a dynamic property influenced by training data distributions, alignment strategies, and the specific persona the model is instructed to emulate.

While behavioral evaluations like ChainPoll and factual consistency benchmarking provide essential insights into *when* and *how* models hallucinate, they treat the LLM largely as a black box, failing to explain *why* these failures occur at a fundamental, algorithmic level. To bridge this explanatory gap, the research frontier is increasingly shifting towards mechanistic frameworks that investigate the internal representations, attention heads, and activation patterns of LLMs. A prominent example of this mechanistic turn is the exploration of "persona vectors" within a model's high-dimensional activation space. As highlighted in recent literature, researchers at Anthropic have pioneered a framework that identifies specific linear directions in the activation space that correspond directly to distinct behavioral traits, such as sycophancy, malicious behavior, and, crucially, hallucination [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. By isolating these persona vectors, researchers gain the unprecedented ability to monitor the internal state of the model in real-time. This allows for the prediction of hallucinatory outputs before the text is even generated. More importantly, this mechanistic understanding opens the door to "representation engineering" or "activation steering," where the model's internal activations are mathematically nudged away from hallucination-prone directions during inference [Banyas_2025_LLMs]. This approach represents a profound paradigm shift from post-hoc behavioral filtering to white-box interpretability, offering a promising pathway to fundamentally excise hallucinatory behaviors at their source and ensure robust model reliability.
